extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and craft guidance for writing and judging poetry (particularly lyric and didactic poetry): sincerity, imagery, form, satire, use of particulars vs abstractions, and the fittingness of diction and tone. Draws on close reading of Young's work to illustrate standards and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as a poetic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “One of the most striking characteristics of Young is his radical insincerity as a poetic artist.” Sincerity means being true to one’s own mental state and to the true qualities of the object or emotion described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sincere poet never produces effects on the audience at the cost of truthful feeling; insincerity leads to grandiloquence and absurdity. Examples of insincerity producing absurdity are quoted (e.g. “An eye of awe and wonder let me roll, / And roll forever”). Insincerity commonly betrays itself when rhetoric is detached from genuine mental state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer particulars over abstractions to evoke emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Emotion links itself with particulars, and only in a faint and secondary manner with abstractions.” Particular cases rouse sympathy; generalities often leave readers cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To move readers, present special cases or concrete details rather than discursive statements about justice/virtue in the abstract. The essay uses the orator example: discoursing on injustice in general leaves audience cold; stating a special case makes every heart throb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid grandiloquence and effects-seeking diction
rubrics_metrics.description: “The source of all grandiloquence is the want of taking for a criterion the true qualities of the object described or the emotion expressed.” Grandiloquence aims at producing a certain audience effect rather than expressing truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for inflated images or statements that cannot be realized imaginatively (e.g. “His hand the good man fixes on the skies…”) and avoid writing that prioritizes theatrical 'sublimity' over fidelity. Grandiloquence often arises when a writer treats abstractions as if they were immediate objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and mastery of rhyme (use blank verse for certain effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Young’s “want of mastery in rhyme is especially a drawback… blank verse is verse unfallen, uncurst; verse reclaimed… in the true language of the gods.” Rhyme can constrain and betray art when not well handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form appropriate to the intended effect: blank verse often better suits lofty or sustained meditation; forced rhyme can introduce superfluous words or inversions that break effect (the ‘Gothic demon’ of rhyme). Ensure technical control when writing rhymed verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal the art — strive for effortless presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The art that conceals art is an absolute requisite.” The best wit and epigram must seem spontaneous and easy, not the result of visible contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid limping or cumbrous rhythm that shows the reader the poet’s mechanical effort (likened to a comedian’s tentative grimaces). The process should be hidden so readers perceive the result, not the making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements of effective satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Good satire should have either ‘terrible vigor’ (indignation), humor that shares fellowship with human nature, or personal bitterness that supplies living particular touches; mere cold epigrams on obvious types are inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing satiric subjects to neat personified vices only; instead cultivate indignation, humane humor, or specific personal detail so the particular becomes universal. Young’s satires fail because they lack genuine indignation, fellow-feeling, or the personal bitterness that yields living touches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overreliance on antithesis and neat epigrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Young’s wit often consists in antithetic combination of ideas—an accessible, clever form but one that can produce coldness and finished neatness rather than deep feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antithesis and epigram are useful devices but should not substitute for character depth or emotional truth. Overuse yields witty but thin portraits and a tendency toward cleverness instead of vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor genuine feeling (complaint) over didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: When the poet shifts from genuine complaint (personal grief) to didactic instruction or theorizing, readers turn from compassionate to critical judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the poet is in truth lamenting, preserve the personal tone; do not convert transient emotional states into abstract moral theories. Didactic passages lessen the reader’s indulgence for morbid exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show virtue and religion in ordinary, concrete human situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Young seldom dwells on virtue or religion as they exist ‘in the emotions of a man dressed in an ordinary coat’—but true sympathy and moral feeling appear in everyday particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict ethical or religious qualities through domestic scenes, small acts of charity, and concrete self‑renunciation rather than from a lofty, telescopic distance. Sympathy is elicited by particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fittingness — match speech and action to subject (common-sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be ‘that fine sense of what is fitting in speech and action’; lacking it produces moral and rhetorical defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tone, diction, and figure suit the emotional and moral situation being described. Avoid grand claims or gestures where modesty or humility would be authentic; use common-sense as an aesthetic check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vulgar or inappropriate imagery in sublime contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to exalt conceptions of Deity or the sublime by vulgar images and comparisons (e.g. ranking God against earthly monarchs) are offensive and undermine solemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain dignity and appropriateness when treating sacred or sublime subjects; inappropriate, familiar, or political comparisons reduce reverence and feel tasteless, as in the quoted ‘Not the great Ottoman…’ passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and originality of subject-matter; avoid repetitious themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Young had ‘only a very few things to say’ repeated throughout; overreliance on a small set of themes weakens a poet’s range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a broader set of images, situations, and ideas rather than recycling the same antitheses (life is vain; death is imminent; immortality; etc.). Freshness of thought sustains interest across long works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural, immediate landscape imagery to enrich poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that turn to lanes, woods, or fields provide sudden relief and are unusually effective in Young’s work because they are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include accessible natural particulars (blossomed trees, brooks, rural scenes) to ground meditative poetry and give readers sensory anchors; the essay quotes a few of Young’s successful natural images as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery must be coherent and imaginable
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of images that cannot be realized imaginatively (e.g. a man’s heart leaning toward the stars) demonstrates that metaphors must be conceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid metaphors and images that the reader cannot form mentally or that violate commonsense imagery. An image should be vivid and yet possible to picture; otherwise it reads as absurd rather than sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate moral tone — avoid simulated vindictiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Simulated or theatrical hatred (e.g. asking that an entire nation be given a grave because of denial of burial rites) displays bad taste and falsity of feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overstep into vindictive or ostentatious moral fury as a rhetorical device; ensure emotional responses in verse are proportionate and authentic rather than performative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and technical precision in epigrams and witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Epigrams and witticisms are peculiarly susceptible to intrusion of a superfluous word or inversion implying constraint, which dissipates the desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep epigrams tight and rhythmically smooth; avoid unnecessary words or awkward inversions caused by forcing rhyme or metre. The electric effect of a witticism depends on technical neatness.
